title: Two distances cannot differ by more than one

prereqs.why: Only the three axioms are available here; the argument uses two of them and nothing else.
This is the statement being proved, and the proof is the content of it.

statement:
**Claim (reverse triangle inequality).** Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space.
For all $x, y, z \in X$,

$$\bigl|\,d(x,y) - d(y,z)\,\bigr| \le d(x,z).$$

The proof below is complete except for the reasons. Choose the justification
for each marked step.

Only the metric axioms are available: positivity, symmetry and the triangle
inequality. Nothing else about $X$ is known.
hints: An inequality of the form $|a| \le b$ is two inequalities in disguise. Write down which two before looking at the metric at all.
To get $d(x,y) - d(y,z) \le d(x,z)$, start from the triangle inequality for $d(x,y)$ and pick the intermediate point that puts $z$ in the middle.
The second half is the first half with $x$ and $z$ interchanged. The only extra step is that $d(z,y)$ and $d(y,z)$ are the same number.

payload.claim: **Claim.** In any metric space $(X,d)$, $\bigl|d(x,y) - d(y,z)\bigr| \le d(x,z)$ for all $x,y,z \in X$.

steps.text: Fix $x, y, z \in X$. It is enough to prove the two inequalities $d(x,y) - d(y,z) \le d(x,z)$ and $d(y,z) - d(x,y) \le d(x,z)$.
$d(z,y) = d(y,z)$, so rearranging gives $d(x,y) - d(y,z) \le d(x,z)$.
$d(y,x) = d(x,y)$, so rearranging gives $d(y,z) - d(x,y) \le d(x,z)$.
Both inequalities hold, so $\bigl|d(x,y) - d(y,z)\bigr| \le d(x,z)$. Since $x,y,z$ were arbitrary, the claim is proved.

choices: $|a| \le b$ holds exactly when $-b \le a \le b$
the triangle inequality, with $z$ as the intermediate point
symmetry of $d$, applied to the pair $z, y$
the triangle inequality, with $x$ as the intermediate point
symmetry of $d$, applied to the pair $y, x$
the limit of a convergent sequence in a metric space is unique
